title: Event Log Interview Review
summary: Fourteen scrolling cards revisit offset semantics, cursor ownership, concurrency, memory and node movement.
audience: Engineers reviewing the event-log interview after implementing a solution.

cards.title: Global IDs and local positions
cards.prompt: A key has IDs [0, 2, 9]. What should an inclusive read from global offset 1 return?
cards.explanation: Compare the offset with event.id: [2, 9] qualify. Filtering by local index > 1 returns only [9]; including ID 0 ignores the lower bound. Skipping one item works for this example by coincidence, not as a general global-offset lookup.

cards.title: Seek once, then walk
cards.prompt: A sorted key log has m events. How can a page of r events avoid scanning its old prefix?
cards.explanation: Lower-bound by global ID, then advance at most r positions. Binary search costs O(log m); the forward page walk costs O(r). filter still examines every entry. A global offset is not a per-key array position; even a valid position with an unbounded slice copies the entire suffix.

cards.title: Who owns currentIndex?
cards.prompt: Two consumers read the same key at different speeds. Where should their read positions live?
cards.explanation: Each consumer keeps its own cursor or a record keyed by consumer identity and key. A shared key cursor lets one reader advance another. The writer nextId allocates global IDs; it does not track either reader’s progress.

cards.title: Sparse anchors
cards.prompt: What does adding a next pointer to every key event guarantee?
cards.explanation: Once positioned, a cursor follows next links in linear time. Arbitrary offsets still need a scan or index. Sparse anchors bound the initial walk. Link objects and pointer chasing can cost more memory and CPU than array references.

cards.title: Publication boundary
cards.prompt: Why is currentIndex++ alone insufficient across independent writers?
cards.explanation: ID allocation, event publication and index updates must be coordinated together. A unique ID does not make its event visible in every index. BigInt is a numeric type, not a lock. A Python multi-step invariant needs explicit coordination; a process-local lock also does not coordinate separate processes.

cards.title: Hot key
cards.prompt: One user owns almost every event. What can adding nodes achieve without changing same-key ownership?
cards.explanation: A key is indivisible under the ownership rule. Move it whole or place other keys elsewhere. Splitting it requires a new contract and ordering policy. Equal event counts do not imply equal memory because payload sizes vary.

cards.title: Retry-safe progress
cards.prompt: A cursor reads through ID 9, but processing fails before success is recorded. Which durable checkpoint policy supports replay?
cards.explanation: Commit nextOffset=10 only after successful processing; distinguish fetched from acknowledged progress. The teaching cursor tracks fetching only. Durable processing needs an explicit acknowledgment policy; checkpointing before a successful effect can lose work. A process pointer is not a restart-safe token. Replaying after an ambiguous effect also requires idempotency.

cards.title: Segment tail boundary
cards.prompt: A cursor opens beyond the current tail of a partly filled block. What must it retain?
cards.explanation: Keep the last block, end slot and requested global lower bound. Later appends may fill that same block; jumping past it skips them. A copied suffix cannot observe appends. New entries below the requested offset must still be skipped.

cards.title: Array cursor
cards.prompt: Where does the array cursor keep position?
cards.explanation: A closure stores a per-consumer numeric index after one binary search. IDs remain bigint; the small array position is a different quantity.

cards.title: Linked cursor
cards.prompt: What happens when a drained linked cursor receives a later append?
cards.explanation: The cursor retains the last visited link and follows its newly populated next pointer. A missing head is rechecked when the first event arrives.

cards.title: Memory budget
cards.prompt: What should a few million events prompt you to estimate?
cards.explanation: Total payload bytes plus event objects, per-key/global references, blocks/anchors, node maps and active pages. Three million 200-byte payloads alone use 600 million bytes before runtime overhead.

cards.title: Migration cost
cards.prompt: Why is moving a simulated bucket cheap?
cards.explanation: All nodes share one heap, so ownership transfers a reference. Actual network migration copies bytes and needs routing versions, a write barrier and safe cutover.

cards.title: Global ordering
cards.explanation: No. This exercise requires one global order across keys. Kafka consumer offsets identify records within a partition, so its normal partition ordering does not supply this global sequence.

cards.title: Bounded pages
cards.prompt: Is slice always an incorrect algorithm?
cards.explanation: No. slice(start, start + limit) after a correct seek copies only the page. slice(offset) is wrong when offset is a global ID and can copy millions of entries. A bounded loop demonstrates explicit control.
